Every release has two steps: upload the new assets, then switch the manifest. The manifest is the file that tells browsers which asset names to load.

**Upload under versioned names.** Each build's assets get unique names, such as `app.3f9c2a.js`. A new upload never overwrites a file that someone might already be loading.

**Upload before the switch.** The manifest switch is the moment the release goes live. As soon as the manifest points to the new names, browsers start requesting those files. If the files aren't there yet, browsers get 404s, and pages break or render without styles. Uploading first means every file the new manifest names already exists when the first browser asks for it. That makes the switch a single, near-instant cutover. Users see either the complete old release or the complete new one, never a mix.

**Keep the old assets.** Browsers don't all pick up the new manifest at the same moment. A user with a page open, or a browser or CDN holding a cached copy of the previous manifest, still requests the old asset names. That includes requests made well after the release, such as lazy-loaded chunks, route changes in a single-page app, or images loaded on scroll. If we deleted the old files, those users would get 404s partway through a session. Keeping them lets every browser finish with the release it started on. It also makes rollback trivial: point the manifest back at the previous names, and nothing needs to be re-uploaded.

Each release deploys in two steps: first we upload every new asset (JS, CSS, images, fonts) under a versioned name, such as a content hash in the filename, and then we update the manifest so pages reference those new names.

The upload comes first so that every file the new manifest references already exists when the manifest goes live. If we switched the manifest first, some browsers would fetch it during the gap and request files that aren't uploaded yet. Those requests would 404 and the page would break. Uploading everything first makes the manifest switch the single moment the release takes effect, and the new version arrives complete.

We keep the old assets because switching the manifest doesn't update browsers that are already running the previous version. A tab opened before the release still holds the old manifest and will keep requesting old files, especially lazy-loaded chunks fetched on navigation. Caches and CDNs may also keep serving the old manifest for a while. If we deleted the old assets, those users would hit 404s partway through a session. Leaving them in place lets old and new versions run side by side until the old clients age out.

Versioned names are what make both steps safe. A new release never overwrites an existing file, so uploading new assets can't affect current users, and old files remain exactly as the old manifest expects them.

Releases happen in two steps, and the order matters.

1. **Upload every new asset under a versioned name.** Each build's files get unique names, such as `app.3f9c2a.js` and `styles.81b07e.css`, so they never overwrite anything already live.
2. **Switch the manifest to point at the new names.** The manifest is the file that tells browsers which asset names make up the current site. Changing it is what actually releases the new version.

**Why the upload comes first:** As soon as the manifest changes, browsers start requesting the files it names. If any of those files weren't uploaded yet, those requests would get 404s and users would see a broken page. Uploading first means every file the new manifest references already exists when the first browser asks for it. The manifest switch is a single small change, so the release takes effect all at once rather than piece by piece.

**Why we keep the old assets:** Some browsers loaded the previous manifest before the switch. They may still have an open tab, a cached page, or lazy-loaded chunks they haven't fetched yet, and they'll keep requesting the old names. If we deleted those files, those users would hit 404s in the middle of a session. Because versioned names never collide, the old and new releases can be served side by side, and each browser gets a consistent set of files. Keeping the old assets also makes rollback simple: point the manifest back at the previous names.

Each release ships in two steps: upload every new asset under a versioned name (for example, `app.3f9c2a.js`), then update the manifest so pages reference those names.

**Why the upload comes first:** the manifest is the only thing that tells browsers which files to fetch. Once it changes, any browser that loads it immediately requests the new names. If those files aren't on the server yet, the browser gets 404s and the page breaks. Uploading first means every name in the new manifest already resolves when browsers see it. Versioned names also mean the new files can't overwrite anything currently in use, so the uploads are invisible to users until the switch.

**Why we keep the old assets:** the switch doesn't reach every browser at once. A browser that loaded the previous manifest, through an open tab, a cached HTML page or a CDN edge that hasn't refreshed, will keep requesting the old names, often lazily as the user navigates. Deleting those files would break the page for those users mid-session. Keeping them lets old and new clients each get a complete, consistent set of files. It also makes rollback a manifest change, since the previous release's assets are still in place.
